$scopeNote: Only ORDINARY (consumer/creditor judgment) wage garnishment is state-overridable here. Federal law — support orders, federal tax levies, federal student loan default — preempts a state's own wage-exemption statute entirely, so nothing in this file ever changes those two calculations in src/garnishment.ts; only 'consumer_creditor' orders consult it. ALL 51 jurisdictions (50 states + DC) are now present in this file as of 2026-09-11 — every one has been actively researched, not left as an unconfirmed absence. A state present with sources but NO formula/prohibition/knownGap block at all (Georgia, Alabama, Louisiana, Michigan, Montana, Ohio, Oklahoma, Rhode Island, Utah, Wyoming) means it was actively researched and CONFIRMED to have no departure from the plain federal CCPA default — a stronger claim than simple absence would have been. A state present with only a `knownGap` note (no `ordinaryGarnishmentProhibited`/`ordinaryGarnishment`/`headOfFamilyOrdinaryGarnishment`/`fullExemption` block) means a real departure or structural nuance IS known to exist but isn't fully modelled (Arkansas's narrow occupational carve-out; Mississippi's 30-day timing rule; New Hampshire's trustee-process mismatch with this engine's standing-order model) — computed against the federal default in the meantime, but disclosed rather than silent. Seven distinct formula SHAPES exist in `GarnishmentFormula` (src/registry.ts): capFractions (+ an optional minimum-wage floor, a state-legislated flat-dollar floor, a per-dependent reduction, or an excess-fraction scale-down), cliff-bracket tiers keyed on minimum-wage multiples or a fixed gross-weekly dollar line, marginal monthly brackets, a poverty-guideline income tier, and Iowa's own cumulative-annual-dollar-cap layer (`annualCapTiers`) — the only shape that caps across MULTIPLE paychecks rather than one at a time.

Cross-corroborated by the statute text itself (via Justia, 403-blocked from a direct fetch this pass but readable through search synthesis) and multiple independent consumer-law summaries, all agreeing on 20%/40%/48x with no dissent.

sources.title: California Department of Industrial Relations — state minimum wage $16.90/hr effective 2026-01-01
sources.verifiedBy: Directly fetched from DIR's own page, which states the figure and effective date verbatim.

CA.$note: WIRED 2026-09-06 — the first state in this file whose floor test reaches only a FRACTION of the excess over the minimum-wage line rather than the full excess (see GarnishmentFormula.minimumWageExcessFraction's own doc comment, added specifically for this entry). Every other state here (IL/NY/MA/CT/CO/WA/WI/ME/VT/ND/MD/NM/SD/VA/WV/DC below) takes 100% of the excess once the floor is crossed; California takes only 40% of it, which is why 40%/48x is NOT simply 'more protective NY-style 25%/30x' — it changes the SHAPE of the marginal test, not just the numbers. Also disclosed, not modelled: the statute's own text directs using a higher LOCAL minimum wage where one applies (many CA cities and counties set their own, e.g. San Francisco, Emeryville) instead of the $16.90 statewide figure used here — same class of geographic simplification already disclosed for CO/MN/NY/ME's own local-minimum-wage gaps, and for the same reason (workState is a bare 2-letter code with no city/county granularity). This entry is also why tests/garnishment.test.ts's own run() helper had to stop defaulting workState to 'CA': every test written before this pass that omitted workState was unknowingly relying on California having NO override, and would have silently started computing California's real formula instead of the plain federal baseline those tests actually intend to exercise. sources.title: RSA 512:21 — New Hampshire's trustee process: wages earned by the defendant AFTER service of the writ upon the trustee are exempt outright; wages already earned but not yet paid AT THE MOMENT of service are exempt except for an action founded upon a debt on a judgment, in which case up to 50 times the federal minimum hourly wage per week is exempt
sources.verifiedBy: Fetched directly. Quoted verbatim: 'Wages for labor performed by the defendant after the service of the writ upon the trustee' are exempt outright — no exception carved back in for a judgment debt the way the PRE-service wage exemption has one ('wages of the defendant earned before the service of the writ... shall be exempt except in actions founded upon a debt on a judgment,' where instead '50 times the minimum hourly wage... for each week shall be exempt').

NH.knownGap: New Hampshire's trustee process is structurally incompatible with the STANDING, RECURRING wage garnishment order this engine (and every other state in this file) models: RSA 512:21 exempts wages earned AFTER the trustee writ is served OUTRIGHT, with no judgment-debt exception the way the pre-service exemption has one. In effect, a creditor enforcing an ordinary judgment can reach only the SPECIFIC amount the employer already owed the debtor at the single moment of service (itself further exempt up to 50x the federal minimum hourly wage/week, MORE protective than the federal 30x floor) — not an ongoing percentage of every future paycheck the way this engine's per-paycheck GarnishmentOrder.amountOrdered model assumes. A NEW trustee writ would need to be served again to reach a later moment's already-accrued-but-unpaid wages, which this engine has no mechanism to represent (it computes one paycheck's own withholding from a standing order, not a sequence of separately-served one-time writs). Not modelled as `ordinaryGarnishmentProhibited` (a court genuinely CAN reach wages already owed at the moment of service, unlike Texas/Pennsylvania/North Carolina/South Carolina's flat bans) and not modelled as a formula either (there is no ongoing per-paycheck percentage to compute) — disclosed as a structural mismatch between this engine's model and New Hampshire's own mechanism, closest in PRACTICAL EFFECT to a prohibition for a standing payroll garnishment order specifically.
